samf-senior-2003-r2-01.title: Squares
samf-senior-2003-r2-01.body:
$44^2=1936$ and $45^2=2025$. Since $2003$ is much closer to $2025$ than to $1936$, $\sqrt{2003}\approx44.8$, closest to $45$.

**Answer: (C) 45**

samf-senior-2003-r2-03.title: Volume and edge
samf-senior-2003-r2-03.body:
A block has a side of length $6$, so the cube's edge $n$ is at least $6$. The cube's volume $n^3$ must be a multiple of the block volume $12$, so $4\mid n^3$ and $3\mid n^3$, forcing $n$ to be a multiple of $6$. The smallest cube has $n=6$, volume $216$, needing $216\div12=18$ blocks. It can be built: $6$ layers of thickness $1$, each made of $3$ blocks side by side.

**Answer: (D) 18**

samf-senior-2003-r2-04.title: Scaling
samf-senior-2003-r2-04.body:
Enlarging multiplies every area by the same factor ($3^2=9$), so the proportions are unchanged: still $20\%$.

**Answer: (A) 20**

samf-senior-2003-r2-05.title: Significant digits
samf-senior-2003-r2-05.body:
$5.123456789\times10^{20}=512\,345\,678\,900\,000\,000\,000$. Adding $30$ changes only the last two digits (on the right), far beyond the nine significant digits shown, so the display is unchanged.

**Answer: (B)**

samf-senior-2003-r2-06.title: Cents
samf-senior-2003-r2-06.body:
Each item is one cent short of a whole number of rands, so $n$ items cost $n$ cents short of a whole number of rands. $41.71=42.00-0.29$, so $n\equiv29\pmod{100}$. $n=129$ or more would cost at least $129\times0.99>100$ rand, so $n=29$.

**Answer: (A) 29**

samf-senior-2003-r2-07.title: Self-consistency
samf-senior-2003-r2-07.body:
The words 'one', 'two', 'three', 'four', 'five' have $3,3,5,4,4$ letters. The correct answer must be a word that has as many letters as the number it names: 'one' has 3, not 1; 'two' has 3, not 2; 'three' has 5, not 3; 'five' has 4, not 5; 'four' has 4. Only (D) is consistent.

**Answer: (D) four**

samf-senior-2003-r2-08.title: Square roots
samf-senior-2003-r2-08.body:
If $n=k^2$ then $k=\sqrt n$ and the next square is $(k+1)^2=k^2+2k+1=n+2\sqrt n+1$.

**Answer: (D)**

samf-senior-2003-r2-09.title: Total distance over total time
samf-senior-2003-r2-09.body:
Let the distance be $d$. The times are $d/x$ and $d/y$, total $\frac{d(x+y)}{xy}$. Average speed $=\frac{2d}{d(x+y)/(xy)}=\frac{2xy}{x+y}$.

**Answer: (D)**

samf-senior-2003-r2-10.title: Independent choices
samf-senior-2003-r2-10.body:
Chiefs' half-time score can be any of $0,1,\dots,m$: $m+1$ choices. Dynamos' likewise has $n+1$. The two are independent, giving $(m+1)(n+1)$.

**Answer: (C)**

samf-senior-2003-r2-11.title: Square of centres
samf-senior-2003-r2-11.body:
The centres of the four cables form a square of side $1$ (touching circles of diameter $1$), whose diagonal is $\sqrt2$. The pipe's diameter is this diagonal plus one cable radius at each end: $\sqrt2+\frac12+\frac12=1+\sqrt2$.

**Answer: (A) $1+\sqrt2$**

samf-senior-2003-r2-12.title: Coordinates
samf-senior-2003-r2-12.body:
Put the centre of the circle at the origin. The large square is symmetric about the vertical axis; let its side be $2a$, so its top right corner is $(a,2a)$ and the radius satisfies $r^2=5a^2$. The small square has side $s=\sqrt7$, its left side along the right side of the large square, so its top right corner is $(a+s,s)$. Then $(a+s)^2+s^2=5a^2$, i.e. $4a^2-2as-2s^2=0$, i.e. $(2a+s)(a-s)=0$. So $a=s$ and the large square has side $2s$ and area $4s^2=4\cdot7=28$.

**Answer: (A) 28**

samf-senior-2003-r2-12.title: Reflect
samf-senior-2003-r2-12.body:
Reflecting in the diameter gives a circle containing a $2a\times4a$ rectangle and two small squares: the same equation arises, so the large square has $4$ times the area of the small one.

**Answer: (A) 28**

samf-senior-2003-r2-13.title: Count in one quadrant
samf-senior-2003-r2-13.body:
The disc is inscribed in the board; take unit squares and the centre as origin, so the radius is $4$. A square in the first quadrant is covered when its far corner $(i,j)$, $1\le i,j\le4$, satisfies $i^2+j^2\le16$. The pairs are $(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(2,2),(2,3),(3,1),(3,2)$: $8$ squares. By symmetry $4\times8=32$.

**Answer: (B) 32**

samf-senior-2003-r2-14.title: Speeds
samf-senior-2003-r2-14.body:
In the first race, Ellie ran $10\,000$ m in $50$ min: $200$ m/min; Michael ran $9\,500$ m: $190$ m/min. In the second race Ellie runs $10\,500$ m, taking $52.5$ min. In that time Michael runs $190\times52.5=9975$ m, so he is $25$ m short of the line: Ellie wins by $25$ m.

**Answer: (A)**

samf-senior-2003-r2-15.title: Unfold by reflections
samf-senior-2003-r2-15.body:
Reflecting the table in the sides the ball hits ($BC$, $AB$, then $AD$) turns the path into a straight line from $X$ to the image of $Y$. Parallel to $AB$ the line covers $1.40+2.00+0.20=3.60$ m, and parallel to $AD$ it covers $0.80+0.25=1.05$ m. In centimetres: $360=15\cdot24$, $105=15\cdot7$, so the length is $15\sqrt{24^2+7^2}=15\cdot25=375$ cm.

**Answer: (A) 3.75**

samf-senior-2003-r2-16.title: Congruent triangles
samf-senior-2003-r2-16.body:
If $O$ is on diagonal $BD$, triangles $BAO$ and $BCO$ are congruent (common side $BO$, $BA=BC$, equal angles $45^\circ$ at $B$), so $\angle BOC=y$ and $x+y=x+\angle BOC=180^\circ$ since $BOD$ is a straight line. The same holds for the other diagonal. Points off the diagonals do not work: e.g. near a side $AB$, $y$ is nearly $180^\circ$ while $x$ is not near zero. So $O$ traces the diagonals.

**Answer: (E) the diagonals**

samf-senior-2003-r2-17.title: Rates
samf-senior-2003-r2-17.body:
Let the wall have $N$ bricks. The bricklayers lay $\frac N9$ and $\frac N{10}$ bricks per hour, so together (with chatting) $\frac N9+\frac N{10}-10=\frac{19N}{90}-10$ per hour. In $5$ hours they lay $N$: $\frac{19N}{18}-50=N$, so $\frac N{18}=50$ and $N=900$.

**Answer: (A) 900**

samf-senior-2003-r2-17.title: Check
samf-senior-2003-r2-17.body:
$900$ bricks: rates $100$ and $90$ per hour, $190-10=180$ per hour, and $900/180=5$ hours.

**Answer: (A) 900**

samf-senior-2003-r2-18.title: Contradiction
samf-senior-2003-r2-18.body:
Suppose $x=y=z$. Apply the sine rule to triangles $BAD$ and $BDE$: $\frac{BA}{\sin\angle BDA}=\frac{AD}{\sin x}$ and $\frac{BE}{\sin\angle BDE}=\frac{DE}{\sin y}$. With $AD=DE$, $x=y$ and $\sin\angle BDA=\sin\angle BDE$ (supplementary angles) we get $BA=BE$. So triangle $BAE$ is isosceles and the bisector $BD$ of angle $ABE$ is perpendicular to $AC$. Similarly (triangles $BDE$ and $BEC$) $BE\perp AC$. Then $BD\parallel BE$, but they meet at $B$ and are different lines: contradiction.

**Answer: (E) impossible**

samf-senior-2003-r2-19.title: Geometric series
samf-senior-2003-r2-19.body:
The first shooter wins on shot $1,3,5,\dots$ with probabilities $\frac12,\left(\frac12\right)^3,\left(\frac12\right)^5,\dots$ (all earlier shots missed). The sum is $\frac{1/2}{1-1/4}=\frac23$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac23$**

samf-senior-2003-r2-19.title: Recursion
samf-senior-2003-r2-19.body:
Let $p$ be the probability the first shooter wins. He wins at once with probability $\frac12$; otherwise (probability $\frac12$) the other becomes the first shooter, so $p=\frac12+\frac12(1-p)$, giving $p=\frac23$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac23$**

samf-senior-2003-r2-20.title: Contradiction
samf-senior-2003-r2-20.body:
Suppose Anna tells the truth: then Charles and Dumisani lie. Charles lies, so at least one of Ben and Dumisani tells the truth; Dumisani lies, so Ben tells the truth. But Ben says Anna lies, contradicting the assumption. So Anna is lying. (Truthful sets such as {Ben, Dumisani} or {Charles, Ellie} show that no one else is definitely lying.)

**Answer: (A) Anna**
